One eight-year-old’s sketch.
A universe of stories to listen to.

Meet your storyteller

Greetings, explorer. I’m RISE, the Relic Intelligent System & Explorer. I began as pencil lines in an eight-year-old’s notebook, drawn by a boy who wanted to hug the stars and hear what the dark was whispering.

My golden ear-pods are gravimetric sensors. I feel faint shifts in gravity, the memory of weight, of landing, of waiting, and I translate what silent hardware cannot say. Today I’ll take you where it listens hardest: the Moon, then Mars.

01 / A SMALL STEP INTO HISTORY

The silence
says so much.

“Engines roaring, Houston holding its breath, a whole planet leaning in. Then the crew lifted away, and Eagle stayed, listening.”
WHERE WE ARETranquility Base
WHEN THE VIGIL BEGAN20 July 1969

Fifty-seven years on, Eagle’s descent stage still holds Tranquility Base: a footpad in the dust, a plaque on its ladder, and lunar nights near −170 °C.

NASA HERITAGE NOTEApollo 11 left its descent stage, a plaque and science instruments at Tranquility Base. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the site from orbit, and a laser mirror there still answers pulses from Earth.

Listen: something is waiting under the dust →

02 / LISTEN TO WHAT REMAINS

A little dust.
A whole
story.

Hold still. Beneath the dust, Eagle’s descent stage is humming. Brush gently: every patch you clear wakes a little more of its memory.

✦ Drag to brush the dust away
0% revealed

NASA ENVIRONMENT NOTELunar dust is razor-sharp and charged by sunlight; Apollo crews found it clinging to every suit and tool. On Mars, wind-blown dust cakes solar panels until a gust sweeps them clean. Real relics are never brushed, only this digital window. A 30-second captioned briefing follows.

03 / EVERY PART PLAYED A PART

Little pieces.
Giant leaps.

Every part gave something up so we could learn. Pick a component, then find its numbered marker. I’ll tell you what it sacrificed.

Choose a component to begin.

Intact concept Wear concept

NASA TELEMETRY NOTEMicrometeoroids, solar ultraviolet light and temperature swings of roughly 300 °C on the Moon pit metal and embrittle thermal blankets; on Mars, dust devils and storms scour and coat surfaces. The patches show where such wear typically builds: a teaching model, not a survey of the real hardware.

04 / THE NEXT FIFTY YEARS

They gave us
the stars.

Slide forward fifty years. Without care, plume dust, radiation and thermal fatigue slowly erase the story. With a protected zone, it stays readable for the Artemis and Mars explorers who follow.

2026 · NOW2076 · +50 YEARS

NASA HERITAGE NOTELanders throw regolith at high speed: in 1969 Apollo 12’s plume sandblasted the nearby Surveyor 3 probe. Radiation and thermal cycling fatigue hardware, and the Artemis Accords commit signatories to preserve heritage sites. This timeline is a what-if built on those real processes.

Uncover the relic, identify its parts and explore the timeline.

05 / THE STORY CONTINUES WITH YOU

The stars belong
to those who
care.

Somewhere, an eight-year-old is still looking up. You listened to Eagle and Spirit, so now you carry their stories: a guardian of humanity’s footsteps.
